## Introduction

### Business Problem

Congress ended federal funding for public broadcasting in 2025, and PBS Utah now expects a recurring shortfall of about $2 million per year. Major donors, people who give $1,200 or more in a fiscal year, are a small share of donors but a large share of donor revenue. PBS Utah does not have a reliable, data-driven way to find which current non-major donors are most likely to become major donors, or at what giving level.

The project will produce a ranked prospect list that development staff can work through. A classification model will estimate each eligible donor's probability of reaching $1,200 or more within 12 months (immediate priority) and within 3 to 5 years (long-term nurture), along with the most likely giving tier ($1,200, $2,000, or $5,000 and up). Major donor status is counted per person, except that a couple whose combined giving reaches $1,200 counts as one major donor. Success will be judged by backtesting on earlier years, and the model has to beat a simple ranking by prior-year giving at a list of 1,000 donors, which is about what the officer cultivation program can work in a year. Results will be reported for all eligible donors and separately for donors who have never been major donors.

### Target and Unit of Analysis

- **Unit of analysis:** one person at the end of a fiscal year t (June 30), called a donor-year. A donor-year is eligible if the person gave in FY t and was not a major donor in FY t. Organizations are not units, and every feature uses only information dated on or before June 30 of FY t.
- **Target:** whether the person becomes a major donor, meaning $1,200 or more of their own giving and soft credits in a fiscal year (or a couple reaching $1,200 together), in FY t+1 for the 12 month outcome, or in any year from FY t+1 to FY t+3 or FY t+5 for the longer outcomes.
- **Secondary target:** the tier reached in the conversion year: $1,200, $2,000, or $5,000 and up.

### How the EDA Changed the Framing

The business problem above is the revised version. The original statement was written before we looked at the data, and the EDA changed it in several ways. The final section lists every change with its evidence.

- Major giving is rarer than the business case said: about 0.3% of donors and 8% of individual giving, not 1% and 19%.
- Prior-year giving alone already ranks about 75% of next-year converters into a list of 1,000, so the original target of 25% of converters in the top 10% would not show that a model adds anything. The bar became the prior-year ranking at the list size officers can actually work.
- About half of converters are former major donors, whom staff likely know already, so results are reported separately for never-major donors.
- Too few donors reach $5,000 or more to support five tiers, so the tiers were reduced to three.
- The University of Utah capacity fields turned out to encode PBS giving, so there is no outside capacity measure.
- Officer contact changes the outcome, and the FY2026 influx changes the conversion rate, so both shaped the validation design.

### Purpose of This Analysis

Each of the four team members completed an individual EDA. The four reached many of the same conclusions but used different definitions for who is eligible, how copy rows and legacy gifts are handled, and how models should be validated, so their headline numbers did not match. The team compared the four, agreed on one set of definitions, and this notebook applies them to the data in a single pass. It also brings in the strongest piece of each individual EDA:

- **Erin:** donor-clustered bootstrap intervals, a lapsed-donor segment, giving-threshold rules as baselines, and legacy history indicators.
- **Benjamin:** content-based cleaning rules, the decoding of the snapshot and University of Utah fields, and the checks on the FY2026 influx.
- **Kate:** the master data dictionary and the split of the cultivation effect before and after program adoption.
- **Samantha:** the time-aware eligibility rule, the rule that a response counts when it is dated, and the separation of raw and cleaned tables with an audit trail.

The individual EDAs remain available in each member's repository, and the appendix describes each member's contributions and the team's use of AI tools. This notebook does not fit a model. It sets up the data, the target, the baselines, and the validation design that the modeling phase will use.

### Agreed Decisions

The table summarizes the definitions used throughout this notebook. Each one is explained and checked in the section where it first matters.

| # | Topic | Agreed rule |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Copy rows | Removed with content-based rules: a row with a broken link or a $0 amount that has an otherwise identical valid row. The copy labels in the row IDs are used only to check the rules. |
| 2 | Eligible population | Donors who gave in fiscal year t and were not major that year. Lapsed donors, who gave in FY t-1 or FY t-2 but not FY t, are reported as a separate segment. |
| 3 | Former major donors | Kept in the eligible population, flagged, and reported separately from never-major donors. |
| 4 | Legacy gifts | Credited to the first listed person, with gifts listing a spouse flagged. Legacy history measures are kept alongside the amounts. |
| 5 | Snapshot years | FY2021 to FY2025, with legacy giving history behind each snapshot. |
| 6 | Repeat solicitations | Kept as repeat solicitations under the same marketing code. |
| 7 | Evidence for added signal | A feature adds signal only if it separates converters within bands of prior-year giving. |
| 8 | Cultivation contact | Contact flags are used in training only, and lists are scored with contact switched off. Results are also reported for donors who were not contacted. Operational and uplift models are out of scope. |
| 9 | Validation | Rolling time-based tests on cohorts whose outcomes end before FY2026, with spouses in the same fold. The FY2025 cohort is used only for final training and reported once as a labeled check. |
| 10 | Baselines | Prior-year giving (the bar to beat), with a "former major or $500" rule as a second check the model should also clear, officer selection measured on held-out donors, a three-part recency, frequency, and value score, and giving-threshold rules. Ties at the list cutoff are split evenly. |
| 11 | Uncertainty | Donor-clustered bootstrap intervals for rates, recall, and lift. |
| 12 | Pipeline | One shared Python build script, with the master data dictionary in the appendix. |
| 13 | Data-quality reporting | Data issues are described where they affect the analysis. |
| 14 | Business problem statement | The team's revisions are summarized in the final section. |
| 15 | Household rule | Major status is per person, but a couple whose combined giving reaches $1,200 counts as one major donor. Both spouses are labeled as converted, and the couple is counted once. |

: Agreed decisions used throughout this notebook

## Data Setup

This notebook combines the four individual EDAs into one analysis. All cleaning and panel construction happens in a single shared script, `build_panel.py`, so every section works from the same tables and the same definitions. The script applies the cleaning and eligibility rules the team agreed on, which are described in the sections that follow. On the first run it converts each raw CSV to a Parquet file in `data_cache/`, and later runs read the Parquet files.

```{python}
#| label: setup

from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
from plotnine import *

import build_panel as bp

# the raw release sits one folder up; the cache lives next to this notebook
RAW = Path("../tables")
CACHE = Path("data_cache")

raw = bp.load_tables(RAW, CACHE)                 # raw tables, typed and snake-cased
clean, audit = bp.clean_tables(raw)              # shared cleaning rules
person_years = bp.build_person_years(clean)      # one row per person per fiscal year
cohorts = bp.build_cohorts(person_years)         # eligible and lapsed donors at each snapshot

# formatting helpers for inline numbers in the text
def n(x):
    return f"{x:,.0f}"

def pct(x, d=1):
    return f"{100 * x:.{d}f}%"

def pp(x, d=2):
    # a difference between two rates, in percentage points
    return f"{100 * x:.{d}f}"

def usd(x):
    return f"${x:,.0f}"

HEADER_NAMES = {"t": "FY t", "fy": "FY", "n_unique": "Distinct values", "dtype": "Type"}
HEADER_WORDS = (("_fy_t_", "_FY t_"), ("_fy26_", "_FY2026_"), ("_fy25_", "_FY2025_"), ("_fy2021_", "_FY2021_"),
                ("_fy_", "_FY_"), ("_ci_", "_CI_"), ("_uofu_", "_UofU_"), ("_pbs_", "_PBS_"), ("_rfv_", "_RFV_"))

def readable(col):
    # snake_case column name to a readable table header
    if col in HEADER_NAMES:
        return HEADER_NAMES[col]
    text = f"_{col}_"
    for old, new in HEADER_WORDS:
        text = text.replace(old, new)
    text = text.strip("_").replace("_", " ")
    return text[0].upper() + text[1:]

def show(df, pct_cols=(), pct_digits=1, caption=None):
    # render a polars frame as a captioned html table, keeping year columns free of separators
    out = df.with_columns([
        pl.col(c).map_elements(lambda v: f"{100 * v:.{pct_digits}f}%", return_dtype=pl.String) for c in pct_cols
    ])
    year_cols = ("fy", "fiscal_year", "first_fy", "last_fy", "t", "cohort", "last_cohort", "outcome_year")
    out = out.with_columns([pl.col(c).cast(pl.String) for c in out.columns if c in year_cols])
    out = out.rename({c: readable(c) for c in out.columns})
    styled = out.to_pandas().style.format(thousands=",", precision=2, na_rep="").hide(axis="index")
    return styled.set_caption(caption) if caption else styled

_ = theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(figure_size=(8, 4)))  # assign so the old theme is not printed
```

The shared build produces `{python} n(person_years.height)` person-years for `{python} n(person_years["constituent_id"].n_unique())` people and `{python} n(cohorts.height)` cohort rows across all snapshots and outcome windows.

## Data Sources and Cleaning

### The Tables

The release has nine tables. Giving comes from three of them: Unite payments (FY2021 on), legacy Team Approach payments (before FY2021), and soft credits, which record gifts paid by donor-advised funds and other organizations on a person's behalf. The other tables describe constituents, solicitations, Passport viewing, and the cultivation program.

```{python}
#| label: table-inventory

# rows, columns, and fiscal-year coverage of each raw table
def fy_span(df, col, is_fy=False):
    years = df[col] if is_fy else df.select(bp.fiscal_year(col))[col]
    return f"FY{years.min()} to FY{years.max()}"

inventory = pl.DataFrame([
    {"table": "constituents_w_memberships", "rows": raw["constituents_w_memberships"].height, "one row per": "constituent", "coverage": "snapshot at end of FY2026"},
    {"table": "unite_payments", "rows": raw["unite_payments"].height, "one row per": "payment", "coverage": fy_span(raw["unite_payments"], "credit_date")},
    {"table": "team_approach_legacy_payments", "rows": raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"].height, "one row per": "legacy gift", "coverage": fy_span(raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"], "gift_date")},
    {"table": "soft_credits", "rows": raw["soft_credits"].height, "one row per": "soft credit", "coverage": fy_span(raw["soft_credits"], "credit_date")},
    {"table": "campaign_codes", "rows": raw["campaign_codes"].height, "one row per": "marketing code", "coverage": "reference table"},
    {"table": "campaign_members", "rows": raw["campaign_members"].height, "one row per": "solicitation", "coverage": fy_span(raw["campaign_members"], "campaign_start_date")},
    {"table": "passport_viewing", "rows": raw["passport_viewing"].height, "one row per": "constituent, year, and genre", "coverage": fy_span(raw["passport_viewing"], "fiscal_year", True)},
    {"table": "cultivation", "rows": raw["cultivation"].height, "one row per": "selected donor and year", "coverage": fy_span(raw["cultivation"], "fiscal_year", True)},
    {"table": "officer_portfolios", "rows": raw["officer_portfolios"].height, "one row per": "officer portfolio", "coverage": "reference table"},
])
# legacy volume before FY1999, when the records become complete
legacy_fy_rows = raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"].group_by(fy=bp.fiscal_year("gift_date")).agg(rows=pl.len())
legacy_pre99_max = legacy_fy_rows.filter(pl.col("fy") < 1999)["rows"].max()

show(inventory, caption="Raw tables in the release: size, unit, and years covered")
```

Legacy records technically start in FY1984, but no year before FY1999 has more than `{python} n(legacy_pre99_max)` gifts, so we treat FY1999 as the start of usable giving history. Solicitation and Passport data only begin in FY2021, which limits how far back the full set of features can reach.

### Copy Rows

The known issues section of the student dictionary describes copy rows in the Unite payment, soft credit, and legacy tables: copies of other rows with one link removed or the amount set to $0, which are not part of anyone's giving. Their IDs carry copy labels, but those labels are meant for checking cleaning rules, not for doing the cleaning. Our rule looks only at the content of each row. A row is a copy when it fails a validity check (a donor, recipient, or campaign code that does not link, an amount of $0 or less, or a legacy gift with no linked constituent) and an otherwise identical valid row exists, matching on every column except the row ID and the field that failed. Exact duplicate soft credits are removed first.

```{python}
#| label: copy-checks

def check_summary(table, flags, df, row_id, amt):
    # rows failing each check, how many have a valid twin, and the dollars involved
    return (
        flags.join(df.select(row_id, amt), on=row_id)
        .group_by("check")
        .agg(rows_failing=pl.len(), with_valid_twin=pl.col("has_valid_twin").sum(), amount=pl.col(amt).sum())
        .with_columns(table=pl.lit(table))
        .select("table", "check", "rows_failing", "with_valid_twin", "amount")
    )

sc_dedup = raw["soft_credits"].unique(maintain_order=True)
legacy_unlinked = raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"].filter(pl.col("constituent_id_1").is_null())
copy_checks = pl.concat([
    check_summary("unite_payments", audit["pay_flags"], raw["unite_payments"], "payment_id", "payment_amount"),
    pl.DataFrame({"table": ["soft_credits"], "check": ["exact duplicate row"],
                  "rows_failing": [audit["sc_exact_duplicates"]], "with_valid_twin": [audit["sc_exact_duplicates"]],
                  "amount": [raw["soft_credits"]["credit_amount"].sum() - sc_dedup["credit_amount"].sum()]}),
    check_summary("soft_credits", audit["sc_flags"], sc_dedup, "credit_id", "credit_amount"),
    pl.DataFrame({"table": ["team_approach_legacy_payments"], "check": ["no linked constituent"],
                  "rows_failing": [audit["legacy_unlinked"]], "with_valid_twin": [audit["legacy_unlinked_copies"]],
                  "amount": [legacy_unlinked["payment_amount"].sum()]}),
], how="vertical_relaxed").sort("table", "check")

failing_without_twin = (copy_checks["rows_failing"] - copy_checks["with_valid_twin"]).sum()
pay_copy_amt = raw["unite_payments"].filter(pl.col("payment_id").is_in(audit["pay_copy_ids"].implode()))["payment_amount"].sum()

show(copy_checks, caption="Rows failing each validity check, and how many have an identical valid twin")
```

```{python}
#| label: copy-label-check

# compare the rows the rules removed with the copy labels
labels = bp.label_agreement(raw, audit)
label_mismatches = (labels["labeled_but_kept"] + labels["removed_but_unlabeled"]).sum()
show(labels, caption="Agreement between the content-based copy rules and the copy labels")
```

Every row that fails a check has a valid twin (`{python} "none" if failing_without_twin == 0 else n(failing_without_twin)` without one), so removing them drops no gift that is not already recorded. The rules remove `{python} n(audit["pay_copy_ids"].len())` Unite payments worth `{python} usd(pay_copy_amt)`, `{python} n(audit["sc_exact_duplicates"] + audit["sc_copy_ids"].len())` soft credits, and `{python} n(audit["legacy_unlinked_copies"])` legacy rows. The second table shows that the rules and the labels agree exactly, with `{python} "no" if label_mismatches == 0 else n(label_mismatches)` mismatches. One individual EDA kept the `{python} n(copy_checks.filter(pl.col("check") == "campaign code not in campaign table")["with_valid_twin"][0])` payments whose campaign code does not link, which counts those gifts twice, another very likely did, and a third removed copies by their labels, so this rule changes their cleaned tables slightly.

### Organizations and Soft Credits

The constituent table includes organization records for the donor-advised fund and other sponsors that pay gifts on a person's behalf. Their payments are the same money that the soft credits assign to people, so counting both would double count it. We identify the organizations by their constituent type and check that their payments match the soft credits.

```{python}
#| label: org-soft-check

orgs = bp.organization_ids(clean["constituents"])
org_fy = (
    clean["payments"].filter(pl.col("donor_id").is_in(orgs.implode()))
    .group_by(fy=bp.fiscal_year("credit_date"))
    .agg(org_payments=pl.len(), org_paid=pl.col("payment_amount").sum())
)
soft_fy = (
    clean["soft_credits"].group_by(fy=bp.fiscal_year("credit_date"))
    .agg(soft_credits=pl.len(), soft_credited=pl.col("credit_amount").sum())
)
org_vs_soft = org_fy.join(soft_fy, on="fy", how="full", coalesce=True).sort("fy")
max_gap = org_vs_soft.select((pl.col("org_paid") - pl.col("soft_credited")).abs().max()).item()

show(org_vs_soft, caption="Organization payments compared with soft credits by fiscal year")
```

There are `{python} n(orgs.len())` organization records, and their payments agree with the soft credits in every fiscal year (largest gap `{python} usd(max_gap)`). A person's fiscal-year giving is therefore their own positive payments plus their soft credits, with organization payments left out. Revenue totals do the reverse and count payments only.

### Repeat Solicitations

```{python}
#| label: repeat-solicitations

cm = clean["campaign_members"]
cm_key = ["constituent_id", "marketing_code", "campaign_start_date"]
cm_exact_dups = cm.height - cm.n_unique()
cm_repeat = cm.filter(pl.struct(cm_key).is_duplicated())
cm_repeat_responses = int(cm_repeat["responded"].sum())
```

The solicitation table has `{python} n(cm_exact_dups)` rows that exactly repeat another row, and `{python} n(cm_repeat.height)` rows share a constituent, marketing code, and fiscal year with another row. `{python} "None" if cm_repeat_responses == 0 else n(cm_repeat_responses)` of those repeats is a response. The student dictionary says a constituent can be solicited more than once under the same code in a year when there is no response, and the table records no contact date that could tell the repeats apart, so we keep them as repeat solicitations. Solicitation adds little signal (see the solicitation section), so this choice has little effect.

### Legacy Gifts

Legacy gifts were recorded by household in the old system, and a row can list more than one linked constituent.

```{python}
#| label: legacy-rule

legacy = clean["legacy"]
legacy_one_person = legacy["constituent_id_2"].is_null().mean()
legacy_spouse_rows = legacy["constituent_id_2"].is_not_null().sum()
legacy_spouse_share_amt = legacy.filter(pl.col("constituent_id_2").is_not_null())["payment_amount"].sum() / legacy["payment_amount"].sum()
legacy_max_ids = legacy.select(pl.sum_horizontal([pl.col(f"constituent_id_{i}").is_not_null() for i in range(1, 8)])).to_series().max()
```

After the copies are removed, `{python} pct(legacy_one_person)` of linked legacy rows name a single person, and no row names more than `{python} n(legacy_max_ids)`. The `{python} n(legacy_spouse_rows)` rows that list a spouse hold `{python} pct(legacy_spouse_share_amt, 2)` of legacy dollars. We credit each legacy gift to the first listed person and flag the spouse rows, which keeps every gift counted once. Crediting both spouses would count those gifts twice, and dropping legacy amounts would lose the giving history that identifies returning major donors and makes the longer outcome windows testable. Legacy history measures such as years given and gift counts are added as features later.

### Columns Not Used

```{python}
#| label: unused-columns

def unused(name, df):
    # columns that are completely blank or hold a single value
    out = []
    for c in df.columns:
        vals = df[c].drop_nulls()
        if df[c].dtype == pl.String:
            vals = vals.filter(vals != "")
        if vals.n_unique() <= 1:
            out.append({"table": name, "column": c, "status": "blank" if vals.len() == 0 else "single value"})
    return out

unused_cols = pl.DataFrame([row for name, df in raw.items() for row in unused(name, df)])
unused_by_table = unused_cols.group_by("table").agg(columns=pl.len()).sort(["columns", "table"], descending=[True, False])
total_cols = sum(df.width for df in raw.values())
show(unused_by_table, caption="Columns that are blank or hold a single value, by table")
```

`{python} n(unused_cols.height)` of the `{python} n(total_cols)` columns are blank or hold a single value, most of them masked fields in the legacy and campaign code tables. Because they do not vary, they cannot help a model and are not used as features. Portfolio capacity is the one exception worth keeping: it is 125 for every portfolio, but it sets the realistic list size of 1,000 donors a year. A few columns that do vary are also left out because they repeat other columns or leak future information; those are covered in the snapshot fields section, and the master data dictionary in the appendix lists the status of every column.

### Missing Values

The columns that are completely blank are covered above. The table below covers the partly missing fields that matter for the analysis, plus two values that act as missing ("Unknown" gender and a year with no Passport record). For each one it gives how much is missing, why, and what we do about it.

```{python}
#| label: missing-values

con_raw = raw["constituents_w_memberships"]
people_raw = con_raw.filter(pl.col("primary_constituent_type") != "Organization")
legacy_raw = raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"]
cm_raw = raw["campaign_members"]
blank_age_orgs = con_raw.filter(pl.col("age").is_null())["primary_constituent_type"].eq("Organization").all()
marital_matches_spouse = (con_raw["marital_status"].is_null() == con_raw["spouse_constituent_id"].is_null()).all()

# eligible donor-years (FY2021 to FY2025) with no Passport record in FY t
elig_recent = cohorts.filter((pl.col("segment") == "active") & (pl.col("window") == 1) & (pl.col("t") >= 2021))
pv_years = raw["passport_viewing"].select("constituent_id", t=pl.col("fiscal_year")).unique()
no_passport = elig_recent.join(pv_years, on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="anti").height / elig_recent.height

def share_missing(s):
    return s.is_null().mean()

def count_missing(s):
    return int(s.is_null().sum())

missing = pl.DataFrame([
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Spouse Constituent ID", "missing": share_missing(con_raw["spouse_constituent_id"]), "rows": count_missing(con_raw["spouse_constituent_id"]),
     "why": "No spouse on file", "handling": "Treated as single: own couple ID, no household combination"},
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Marital Status", "missing": share_missing(con_raw["marital_status"]), "rows": count_missing(con_raw["marital_status"]),
     "why": "Blank exactly when no spouse is on file" if marital_matches_spouse else "Mostly when no spouse is on file",
     "handling": "Dropped; repeats spouse on file"},
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Gender = Unknown", "missing": (people_raw["gender"] == "Unknown").mean(), "rows": int((people_raw["gender"] == "Unknown").sum()),
     "why": "Not recorded; may mark thinner records", "handling": "Kept as its own level"},
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Age, gender, giving group", "missing": share_missing(con_raw["age"]), "rows": count_missing(con_raw["age"]),
     "why": "Blank only for the two organization records" if blank_age_orgs else "Mixed",
     "handling": "Organizations are not units of analysis"},
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Major Donor Class", "missing": share_missing(con_raw["major_donor_class_pbs_utah"]), "rows": count_missing(con_raw["major_donor_class_pbs_utah"]),
     "why": "Blank means never a major donor", "handling": "Dropped; describes FY2026 giving"},
    {"table": "legacy payments", "field": "constituent_id_1", "missing": share_missing(legacy_raw["constituent_id_1"]), "rows": count_missing(legacy_raw["constituent_id_1"]),
     "why": "Copy rows with the link removed", "handling": "Removed by the copy rule"},
    {"table": "legacy payments", "field": "constituent_id_2", "missing": share_missing(legacy_raw["constituent_id_2"]), "rows": count_missing(legacy_raw["constituent_id_2"]),
     "why": "Gift lists one person", "handling": "Gift credited to the first person; spouse rows flagged"},
    {"table": "campaign members", "field": "responded_date, response_type", "missing": share_missing(cm_raw["responded_date"]), "rows": count_missing(cm_raw["responded_date"]),
     "why": "No response to that solicitation", "handling": "Structural, not imputed; responses counted by response date"},
    {"table": "passport viewing", "field": "No record in FY t (eligible donor-years)", "missing": no_passport, "rows": round(no_passport * elig_recent.height),
     "why": "No linked account, no consent, or no viewing; the data cannot tell which", "handling": "Own \"no viewing record\" level, never set to zero viewing"},
    {"table": "officer portfolios", "field": "rollout_fy", "missing": share_missing(raw["officer_portfolios"]["rollout_fy"]), "rows": count_missing(raw["officer_portfolios"]["rollout_fy"]),
     "why": "The one portfolio that never adopted the program", "handling": "Treated as not adopted"},
])
payment_nulls = sum(raw[t][c].null_count() for t in ("unite_payments", "soft_credits") for c in raw[t].columns)
show(missing.select("table", "field", "rows", "missing", "why", "handling"), pct_cols=["missing"], caption="Partly missing fields that matter: how much, why, and how they are handled")
```

Most of the missing values are structural rather than lost data: a blank spouse means no spouse, a blank response date means no response, and a blank major donor class means never major. None of the fields that feed the model is imputed. Two cases need care in modeling. Unknown gender covers about a fifth of people and is kept as its own level, since it may say more about how complete a record is than about the person. A missing Passport year is the more serious gap, because about half of eligible donor-years have no viewing record and the data cannot say why, so any Passport feature carries its own "no viewing record" level. The payment and soft credit tables have no missing values in the fields we use.

### Cleaned Tables

```{python}
#| label: cleaned-summary

cleaned = pl.DataFrame([
    {"table": "unite_payments", "raw_rows": raw["unite_payments"].height, "cleaned_rows": clean["payments"].height},
    {"table": "soft_credits", "raw_rows": raw["soft_credits"].height, "cleaned_rows": clean["soft_credits"].height},
    {"table": "team_approach_legacy_payments", "raw_rows": raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"].height, "cleaned_rows": clean["legacy"].height},
    {"table": "campaign_members", "raw_rows": raw["campaign_members"].height, "cleaned_rows": clean["campaign_members"].height},
]).with_columns(rows_removed=pl.col("raw_rows") - pl.col("cleaned_rows"))
show(cleaned, caption="Rows before and after cleaning")
```

The raw tables are kept unchanged and the cleaned versions are built from them, so every removal can be traced back to the rule that caused it.

## Giving Panel and Eligible Population

### Fiscal-Year Giving

The panel has one row per person per fiscal year in which they gave. A person's giving in a year is the sum of their own Unite payments, their soft credits, and the legacy gifts credited to them, with organization payments left out. Each row also keeps the pieces of that total (recurring and one-time payments, soft credits, legacy amounts, and the share of legacy dollars from gifts that list a spouse), which later sections use as features.

```{python}
#| label: panel-overview

# where each fiscal year's individual giving comes from
source_mix = (
    person_years.filter(pl.col("fy") >= 1999)
    .with_columns(era=pl.when(pl.col("fy") >= 2021).then(pl.lit("FY2021 to FY2026 (Unite)")).otherwise(pl.lit("FY1999 to FY2020 (legacy)")))
    .group_by("era")
    .agg(person_years=pl.len(), people=pl.col("constituent_id").n_unique(),
         unite=pl.col("unite_amt").sum(), soft_credits=pl.col("soft_amt").sum(), legacy=pl.col("legacy_amt").sum())
    .sort("era", descending=True)
)

# donors who give again the next year, around the switch from legacy to Unite
donor_years = person_years.select("constituent_id", "fy")
def retention(fy):
    this_year = donor_years.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy)
    return this_year.join(donor_years.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy + 1), on="constituent_id", how="semi").height / this_year.height
ret_19, ret_20, ret_21 = retention(2019), retention(2020), retention(2021)

show(source_mix, caption="Where individual giving comes from in the legacy and Unite eras")
```

From FY2021 on, individual giving comes from Unite payments and soft credits, and before that from legacy gifts. The switch between the two systems does not break donors' histories: the share of donors who give again the next year moves smoothly from `{python} pct(ret_19)` (FY2019 to FY2020) to `{python} pct(ret_20)` (FY2020 to FY2021) and `{python} pct(ret_21)` (FY2021 to FY2022). Legacy history can therefore sit behind each Unite-era snapshot.

### The Household Rule

Major status is counted per person, except that a couple whose combined giving reaches $1,200, when neither spouse does alone, counts as one major donor. Both spouses are labeled as major in that year and share a couple ID, so the couple can be counted once.

```{python}
#| label: household-rule

recent_py = person_years.filter(pl.col("fy") >= 2021)
combined_only_rows = person_years.filter("major_combined_only")
combined_only_couple_years = combined_only_rows.select("couple_id", "fy").unique().height

majors_by_fy = (
    recent_py.filter(pl.col("major"))
    .group_by("fy")
    .agg(people_major=pl.len(), major_units=pl.col("couple_id").n_unique(),
         combined_only=pl.col("major_combined_only").sum())
    .sort("fy")
)
both_individually_major = (
    recent_py.filter(pl.col("major_individual") & pl.col("spouse_id").is_not_null())
    .join(recent_py.filter("major_individual").select(spouse_id=pl.col("constituent_id"), fy="fy"),
          on=["spouse_id", "fy"], how="semi")
    .height
)
show(majors_by_fy, caption="Major donors per year, with couples counted once")
```

In the whole panel, `{python} n(combined_only_couple_years)` couple-year reaches $1,200 only in combination (`{python} n(combined_only_rows.height)` people, in FY`{python} combined_only_rows["fy"][0]`), and `{python} "no" if both_individually_major == 0 else n(both_individually_major)` couples have both spouses major on their own in the same year. The rule therefore changes the count of major donors by one unit, so it matters for correctness more than for the numbers in this data. The `major_units` column counts each couple once, which is the count used for donor shares.

### Eligible Population

At the end of each fiscal year t, the eligible population is every donor who gave that year and was not a major donor that year. Donors who gave in FY t-1 or FY t-2 but not in FY t form a separate lapsed segment. Within both groups, donors who were major in any earlier year, including the legacy years, are flagged as former major donors. A donor converts when they become major (under the household rule) in the outcome window.

```{python}
#| label: eligible-population

c12 = cohorts.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & (pl.col("t") >= 2021))
eligible_summary = (
    c12.group_by("t", "segment")
    .agg(donors=pl.len(), former_majors=pl.col("former_major").sum(), converters=pl.col("converted").sum(),
         in_validation=pl.col("in_validation").first())
    .with_columns(rate=pl.col("converters") / pl.col("donors"))
    .sort("segment", "t")
)
seg = {s: c12.filter(pl.col("segment") == s) for s in ("active", "lapsed")}
active_conv = seg["active"]["converted"].sum()
lapsed_conv = seg["lapsed"]["converted"].sum()
active_val = seg["active"].filter("in_validation")
show(eligible_summary, pct_cols=["rate"], pct_digits=3, caption="Eligible donors and 12 month converters by cohort and segment")
```

From FY2021 to FY2025 there are about `{python} n(round(seg["active"].height / 5, -3))` eligible donors a year and `{python} n(active_conv)` 12 month converters in total. The lapsed segment adds about `{python} n(round(seg["lapsed"].height / 5, -3))` donors a year but only `{python} n(lapsed_conv)` converters, which supports keeping it separate: lapsed donors rarely come back as major donors within a year, and mixing them in would dilute the eligible group. Following the validation decision, only the FY2021 to FY2024 cohorts (`{python} n(active_val["converted"].sum())` active converters) are used to compare models. The FY2025 cohort, whose outcomes fall in FY2026, is used only in final training.

### Reconciling the Four Individual EDAs

The individual EDAs reported different converter counts because they used different eligibility rules and, in one case, different years. Rebuilding each definition from the shared panel shows that the counts all come from the same data.

```{python}
#| label: reconcile

py_major = person_years.select("constituent_id", "fy", "total", "major_individual")
first_fy = person_years.group_by("constituent_id").agg(first_fy=pl.col("fy").min())

def ids(df):
    return df["constituent_id"].unique().implode()

def converters(eligible, t):
    # individual-rule converters: major on their own in FY t+1
    nxt = py_major.filter((pl.col("fy") == t + 1) & pl.col("major_individual"))
    return eligible.filter(pl.col("constituent_id").is_in(ids(nxt))).height

def count(years, rule):
    total = 0
    for t in years:
        major_t = ids(py_major.filter((pl.col("fy") == t) & pl.col("major_individual")))
        gave_t = py_major.filter((pl.col("fy") == t) & ~pl.col("major_individual")).select("constituent_id")
        if rule == "gave in FY t":
            elig = gave_t
        elif rule == "ever gave by FY t":
            elig = first_fy.filter((pl.col("first_fy") <= t) & ~pl.col("constituent_id").is_in(major_t)).select("constituent_id")
        elif rule == "gave in FY t, not major since FY2021":
            since21 = ids(py_major.filter(pl.col("fy").is_between(2021, t - 1) & pl.col("major_individual")))
            elig = gave_t.filter(~pl.col("constituent_id").is_in(since21))
        elif rule == "gave in FY t, never major":
            ever = ids(py_major.filter((pl.col("fy") < t) & pl.col("major_individual")))
            elig = gave_t.filter(~pl.col("constituent_id").is_in(ever))
        total += converters(elig, t)
    return total

reconciliation = pl.DataFrame([
    {"definition": "Agreed: gave in FY t, household rule", "used_by": "this notebook", "cohorts": "FY2021 to FY2025", "converters_12m": active_conv},
    {"definition": "Gave in FY t, per person only", "used_by": "Benjamin, Kate", "cohorts": "FY2021 to FY2025", "converters_12m": count(range(2021, 2026), "gave in FY t")},
    {"definition": "Ever gave by FY t, per person only", "used_by": "Samantha", "cohorts": "FY2021 to FY2025", "converters_12m": count(range(2021, 2026), "ever gave by FY t")},
    {"definition": "Gave in FY t, not major since FY2021", "used_by": "Erin (active donors)", "cohorts": "FY2023 to FY2025", "converters_12m": count(range(2023, 2026), "gave in FY t, not major since FY2021")},
    {"definition": "Gave in FY t, never major in any year", "used_by": "reference", "cohorts": "FY2023 to FY2025", "converters_12m": count(range(2023, 2026), "gave in FY t, never major")},
])
rc = {r["used_by"]: r["converters_12m"] for r in reconciliation.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(reconciliation, caption="Each individual EDA's converter count rebuilt from the shared panel")
```

Each individual EDA's count is reproduced exactly from the shared panel:

- Benjamin's and Kate's `{python} n(rc["Benjamin, Kate"])` converters are the agreed definition without the household rule. The household rule adds `{python} n(active_conv - rc["Benjamin, Kate"])`.
- Samantha's `{python} n(rc["Samantha"])` include everyone who had ever given, so they add `{python} n(rc["Samantha"] - rc["Benjamin, Kate"])` lapsed donors of any length to Benjamin's and Kate's count.
- Erin's `{python} n(rc["Erin (active donors)"])` active converters come from three cohorts and exclude anyone major since FY2021. Of these, `{python} n(rc["Erin (active donors)"] - rc["reference"])` had been major before FY2021, which only shows up when legacy amounts are used. Erin's two lapsed converters come from her own lapsed definition, which is not rebuilt here.

The agreed definition keeps the full giving history (legacy amounts back to FY1999), all five Unite-era cohorts, and former major donors as a flagged group. Samantha's broader rule finds a few more converters, but it does so by adding tens of thousands of long-lapsed donors who almost never convert. Keeping recent lapsed donors as a separate segment captures some of those converters without diluting the main group.

## How Rare Major Giving Is

### Major Donors as a Share of Donors and Revenue

The business case describes major donors as about 1% of the donor file and about 19% of donor revenue. The table checks this for each fiscal year from FY2021 on. Donors are people who gave that year. Major donors are counted in units, so a couple that qualifies only in combination counts once, and revenue is individual giving.

```{python}
#| label: major-share

share_by_fy = (
    person_years.filter(pl.col("fy") >= 2021)
    .group_by("fy")
    .agg(
        donors=pl.len(),
        major_donors=pl.col("couple_id").filter(pl.col("major")).n_unique(),
        revenue=pl.col("total").sum(),
        major_revenue=pl.col("total").filter(pl.col("major")).sum(),
    )
    .with_columns(share_of_donors=pl.col("major_donors") / pl.col("donors"),
                  share_of_revenue=pl.col("major_revenue") / pl.col("revenue"))
    .sort("fy")
)
pooled_share = share_by_fy.select(
    donors=pl.col("major_donors").sum() / pl.col("donors").sum(),
    revenue=pl.col("major_revenue").sum() / pl.col("revenue").sum(),
).row(0, named=True)

show(share_by_fy, pct_cols=["share_of_donors", "share_of_revenue"], pct_digits=2, caption="Major donors as a share of donors and of individual giving")
```

Major donors are `{python} pct(share_by_fy["share_of_donors"].min(), 2)` to `{python} pct(share_by_fy["share_of_donors"].max(), 2)` of donors each year (`{python} pct(pooled_share["donors"], 2)` pooled) and give `{python} pct(share_by_fy["share_of_revenue"].min())` to `{python} pct(share_by_fy["share_of_revenue"].max())` of revenue (`{python} pct(pooled_share["revenue"])` pooled), well below the 1% and 19% in the business case. Benjamin's and Kate's EDAs, the two that checked these figures, found the same gap, and none of the alternative definitions they tried (a $1,000 threshold, combining spouses) closes it. The team's revised problem statement restates these figures from the data.

### Giving Around the $1,200 Line

If many donors gave just below $1,200, crossing the line would be a small step and easy to predict. The bands below show annual giving per person-year from FY2021 on.

```{python}
#| label: giving-bands

edges = [250, 500, 750, 1000, 1200, 1200.01, 2000, 2000.01, 5000, 5000.01]
band_labels = ["under $250", "$250 to $499", "$500 to $749", "$750 to $999", "$1,000 to $1,199", "exactly $1,200",
               "$1,200.01 to $1,999", "exactly $2,000", "$2,000.01 to $4,999", "exactly $5,000", "over $5,000"]
recent = person_years.filter(pl.col("fy") >= 2021)
bands = (
    recent.with_columns(band=pl.col("total").cut(edges, labels=band_labels, left_closed=True).cast(pl.Enum(band_labels)))
    .group_by("band").agg(person_years=pl.len())
)
# show every band, including empty ones, in order
bands = (
    pl.DataFrame({"band": band_labels}).with_columns(pl.col("band").cast(pl.Enum(band_labels)))
    .join(bands, on="band", how="left").with_columns(pl.col("person_years").fill_null(0))
)
recent_majors = recent.filter("major_individual")
exact_tier_share = recent_majors["total"].is_in([1200, 2000, 5000, 10000]).mean()
nonmajor_max = recent.filter(~pl.col("major_individual"))["total"].max()
just_under = recent.filter(pl.col("total").is_between(750, 1200, closed="left")).height
between_tiers = recent.filter((pl.col("total") > 1200) & (pl.col("total") < 2000)).height
at_600 = recent.filter(pl.col("total").is_between(500, 750)).select((pl.col("total") == 600).mean()).item()

show(bands, caption="Person-years by band of annual giving, FY2021 to FY2026")
```

Giving is not smooth around the line. No non-major donor-year exceeds `{python} usd(nonmajor_max)`, only `{python} n(just_under)` fall between $750 and $1,199, and `{python} "none" if between_tiers == 0 else n(between_tiers)` fall strictly between $1,200 and $2,000. `{python} pct(exact_tier_share)` of major donor-years are exactly $1,200, $2,000, $5,000, or $10,000, and `{python} pct(at_600)` of donor-years in the $500 to $749 band are exactly $600. Becoming a major donor is therefore a jump from the regular giving range, not a small step over the line. As later sections show, the donors who make that jump still come mostly from the top of the regular range.

### Conversion Base Rates

The rates below use the eligible population from the previous section. Intervals come from a donor-clustered bootstrap: each resample draws whole couples (or single donors) with replacement, keeping all of their cohort rows together, so repeated appearances of the same donor do not make the estimate look more certain than it is.

```{python}
#| label: base-rates

import numpy as np

def clustered_rate(df, reps=1000, seed=20261009):
    # point estimate and 95% interval, resampling couple_id clusters with replacement
    # sort so the same seed always draws the same couples
    g = df.group_by("couple_id").agg(rows=pl.len(), conv=pl.col("converted").sum()).sort("couple_id")
    rows, conv = g["rows"].to_numpy(), g["conv"].to_numpy()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    m = len(g)
    draws = np.empty(reps)
    for r in range(reps):
        pick = rng.integers(0, m, m)
        draws[r] = conv[pick].sum() / rows[pick].sum()
    return conv.sum() / rows.sum(), np.quantile(draws, 0.025), np.quantile(draws, 0.975)

active = cohorts.filter((pl.col("segment") == "active") & (pl.col("t") >= 2021))
specs = [
    ("12 months", "all eligible", "FY2021 to FY2025", active.filter(pl.col("window") == 1)),
    ("12 months", "never major", "FY2021 to FY2025", active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & ~pl.col("former_major"))),
    ("12 months", "former major", "FY2021 to FY2025", active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("former_major"))),
    ("12 months", "all eligible", "FY2021 to FY2024 (validation)", active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("in_validation"))),
    ("12 months", "lapsed segment", "FY2021 to FY2025", cohorts.filter((pl.col("segment") == "lapsed") & (pl.col("window") == 1) & (pl.col("t") >= 2021))),
    ("within 3 years", "all eligible", "FY2021 to FY2023", active.filter(pl.col("window") == 3)),
    ("within 5 years", "all eligible", "FY2021", active.filter(pl.col("window") == 5)),
]
rate_rows = []
for outcome, group, cohorts_used, df in specs:
    est, lo, hi = clustered_rate(df)
    rate_rows.append({"outcome": outcome, "group": group, "cohorts": cohorts_used, "donor_years": df.height,
                      "converters": int(df["converted"].sum()), "rate": est, "ci_low": lo, "ci_high": hi})
base_rates = pl.DataFrame(rate_rows)
br = {(r["outcome"], r["group"], r["cohorts"]): r for r in base_rates.iter_rows(named=True)}
r12 = br[("12 months", "all eligible", "FY2021 to FY2025")]
r12_never = br[("12 months", "never major", "FY2021 to FY2025")]
r12_former = br[("12 months", "former major", "FY2021 to FY2025")]

show(base_rates, pct_cols=["rate", "ci_low", "ci_high"], pct_digits=3, caption="Conversion base rates with couple-clustered 95% intervals")
```

Conversion is rare. `{python} pct(r12["rate"], 2)` of eligible donors become major donors the next year (95% interval `{python} pct(r12["ci_low"], 2)` to `{python} pct(r12["ci_high"], 2)`), about `{python} n(r12["converters"] / 5)` people a year. Former major donors convert at `{python} pct(r12_former["rate"])`, compared with `{python} pct(r12_never["rate"], 3)` for never-major donors, and they account for `{python} pct(r12_former["converters"] / r12["converters"], 0)` of converters while being `{python} pct(r12_former["donor_years"] / r12["donor_years"])` of eligible donors. This is why results must be reported separately for never-major donors: staff likely already know their lapsed major donors, and a list that mostly finds them would look strong without adding much. The intervals are narrowest for the pooled 12 month rate and widest for the lapsed segment, which rests on only `{python} n(br[("12 months", "lapsed segment", "FY2021 to FY2025")]["converters"])` converters. The 5 year rate comes from a single cohort, so its interval reflects donor variation within that cohort but not variation between years.

### Tiers Reached at Conversion

```{python}
#| label: conversion-tiers

# tier in the conversion year, using the couple's combined giving when only the couple qualifies
tier_basis = person_years.with_columns(
    tier_total=pl.when(pl.col("major_combined_only")).then(pl.col("total") + pl.col("spouse_total")).otherwise(pl.col("total"))
).with_columns(conv_tier=pl.col("tier_total").cut(bp.TIERS, labels=bp.TIER_LABELS, left_closed=True).cast(pl.Enum(bp.TIER_LABELS)))

conv_tiers = (
    active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("converted"))
    .select("constituent_id", fy=pl.col("t") + 1)
    .join(tier_basis.select("constituent_id", "fy", "conv_tier"), on=["constituent_id", "fy"])
    .group_by("conv_tier").agg(converters=pl.len())
    .with_columns(share=pl.col("converters") / pl.col("converters").sum())
    .sort("conv_tier")
)
tier_n = {str(r["conv_tier"]): r["converters"] for r in conv_tiers.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(conv_tiers, pct_cols=["share"], caption="Tier reached by 12 month converters")
```

Of the `{python} n(r12["converters"])` 12 month converters, `{python} n(tier_n.get("$1,200", 0))` reach the $1,200 tier, `{python} n(tier_n.get("$2,000", 0))` reach $2,000, and only `{python} n(tier_n.get("$5,000+", 0))` reach $5,000 or more. This supports the agreed three-tier scheme, and it means the tier model is mostly a choice between $1,200 and $2,000, with too few cases above that to model separately.

### Summary for Modeling

- The 12 month conversion rate is about `{python} pct(r12["rate"], 2)`, so models should be judged on ranking measures at a fixed list size, not accuracy.
- Former major donors are a small, high-converting group and are reported separately.
- Major giving is a jump to a tier amount, so the model has to find donors who are likely to make that jump, not donors who are close to the line.
- Single-cohort results are noisy, and clustered intervals should accompany every rate, recall, and lift reported in modeling.

## Signals From Giving History

This section asks which parts of a donor's giving history add information beyond how much they gave in FY t. Every feature is measured at the end of FY t from gifts dated on or before June 30 of that year, so nothing comes from the outcome years. Choosing features is part of model selection, so the section uses only the validation cohorts (FY2021 to FY2024) and leaves out the FY2025 cohort. The main outcome is the 12 month window, with a 3 year check at the end. The lapsed segment is left out because it has too few converters to compare features.

```{python}
#| label: giving-features

gifts = bp.individual_gifts(clean)
PRIOR_BANDS = ["$60 or less", "$61 to $120", "$121 to $240", "$241 to $500", "over $500"]

def with_features(rows):
    # giving-history features at the end of FY t plus the prior-year giving band
    return rows.join(bp.giving_features(rows, person_years, gifts), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left").with_columns(
        band=pl.col("prior_total").cut([60, 120, 240, 500], labels=PRIOR_BANDS).cast(pl.Enum(PRIOR_BANDS))
    )

feat12 = with_features(active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("in_validation")))
feat3 = with_features(active.filter((pl.col("window") == 3) & pl.col("in_validation")))
base12 = feat12["converted"].mean()
```

### Prior-Year Giving

```{python}
#| label: prior-year-bands

band_rows = []
for b in PRIOR_BANDS:
    d = feat12.filter(pl.col("band") == b)
    est, lo, hi = clustered_rate(d)
    band_rows.append({"prior_year_giving": b, "donor_years": d.height, "converters": int(d["converted"].sum()),
                      "rate": est, "ci_low": lo, "ci_high": hi,
                      "never_major_rate": d.filter(~pl.col("former_major"))["converted"].mean()})
prior_bands = pl.DataFrame(band_rows).with_columns(
    share_of_donors=pl.col("donor_years") / pl.col("donor_years").sum(),
    share_of_converters=pl.col("converters") / pl.col("converters").sum(),
)
pb = {r["prior_year_giving"]: r for r in prior_bands.iter_rows(named=True)}
low_bands = prior_bands.filter(pl.col("prior_year_giving").is_in(PRIOR_BANDS[:3])).select(
    pl.col("share_of_donors", "share_of_converters").sum()).row(0, named=True)

show(prior_bands, pct_cols=["rate", "ci_low", "ci_high", "never_major_rate", "share_of_donors", "share_of_converters"], pct_digits=2, caption="12 month conversion by prior-year giving band, FY2021 to FY2024 cohorts")
```

```{python}

#| fig-height: 4

def percent_labels(breaks):
    return [f"{100 * b:.0f}%" for b in breaks]

band_plot = []
for b in PRIOR_BANDS:
    d = feat12.filter(pl.col("band") == b)
    for group, dd in [("All eligible", d), ("Never major", d.filter(~pl.col("former_major")))]:
        est, lo, hi = clustered_rate(dd)
        band_plot.append({"band": b.replace("$", r"\$"), "group": group, "rate": est, "lo": lo, "hi": hi})
band_pd = pl.DataFrame(band_plot).to_pandas()
band_pd["band"] = pd.Categorical(band_pd["band"], categories=[b.replace("$", r"\$") for b in PRIOR_BANDS], ordered=True)

(
    ggplot(band_pd, aes("band", "rate", fill="group"))
    + geom_col(position=position_dodge(width=0.8), width=0.75)
    + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin="lo", ymax="hi"), position=position_dodge(width=0.8), width=0.25)
    + scale_y_continuous(labels=percent_labels)
    + labs(x="Giving in FY t", y="Converted in FY t+1", fill="",
           title="12 month conversion rises steeply with prior-year giving",
           subtitle="FY2021 to FY2024 cohorts, 95% couple-clustered intervals")
```
